frames.narration: A user in Frankfurt likes a post. Latency-based routing sends the request to the EU region, 12 ms away, instead of the US region 90 ms away.
The EU region commits the like in its own database, which takes a few milliseconds, and answers at once. The response carries a version token, EU sequence 9,017, which the app keeps.
The change record is put on the replication stream with the EU sequence number. It is sent to the US and Asia regions in parallel and does not delay the user.

At almost the same moment a user in Virginia liked the same post. Each region has applied its own like and now receives the other's. The likes are a counter CRDT with one slot per region, so the merge takes the larger value of each slot: nothing is lost and no region has to decide who was first.

All three regions now show 42 likes, 30 from the US plus 12 from the EU. Had the likes been a single value with last-writer-wins, one of the two concurrent updates would have overwritten the other and the post would show 41.

The user then reloads and a network change routes the request to the US region. It has applied EU up to 9,017, which is what the token asks for, so it answers with the like included. Had it been behind, it would have waited a moment or sent the user back to the EU region.
